To botch something means to do it so poorly, carelessly, or clumsily that the result is ruined, messy, or a complete failure. When you botch something, you had the chance to do it properly — but through lack of skill, carelessness, or rushing, you made a mess of it.

Think of it this way: imagine a tailor who is supposed to fix a small tear in your jacket. Instead, he sews it crookedly, cuts the fabric in the wrong place, and leaves the jacket looking worse than before. He botched the repair.

"Botch" carries a strong sense of incompetence and disappointment. It is not just about failing — it is about failing in a way that was avoidable. When someone botches something, we feel that a reasonably careful or skilled person would have done it right. There is often a sense of frustration attached to it, either from the person who did it or the person affected by it.

This is what separates "botch" from a simple word like "fail." You can fail at something because it was genuinely difficult or because luck was against you. But when you botch something, the failure is on you — it was mishandled, fumbled, or bungled.

• botch — the base form: "Don't botch this."
  • botches — third person singular: "He always botches things."
  • botched — past tense, and also used as an adjective: "She botched the interview." / "It was a botched attempt."
  • botching — present participle: "He kept botching every task they gave him."
  • botch up — a very common phrasal verb that means exactly the same thing: "He botched up the whole plan."
  • a botch or a botch-up — noun forms meaning the act or result of botching: "The renovation was a complete botch."

These examples will help you see how the word is used in real situations:

  • The electrician botched the wiring, and now half the lights in the house don't work.
  • She was so nervous that she botched her job interview completely.
  • The government botched its response to the crisis, making everything worse.
  • He tried to bake a cake without reading the recipe carefully and botched it badly.
  • The surgeon botched the procedure, and the patient needed a second operation to correct the damage.
  • They only had one chance to win the match, and they botched it.
  • Stop rushing — you're going to botch the whole thing.
Very Common Collocations (Word Pairs You Will Often See)

Certain words appear alongside "botch" very frequently. Knowing these will help you recognise and use the word naturally:

  • a botched job — when work is done poorly: "The plumber did a botched job on the pipes."
  • a botched attempt — a failed, poorly executed try: "It was a botched attempt at a surprise party."
  • a botched robbery — a robbery that went wrong due to poor planning or execution
  • a botched surgery / a botched operation — a medical procedure that was carried out badly
  • a botched execution — used in journalism and news to describe a punishment carried out incorrectly
  • botch it up — an informal, emphatic version: "I knew he'd botch it up."

The word "botched" (the adjective form) is especially common in news headlines and journalism, where you will see phrases like "botched raid," "botched rescue mission," or "botched investigation."
How It Differs From Similar Words

Several words are close in meaning to "botch" but carry slightly different shades:

  • Ruin — focuses on the damage done to the end result, not necessarily the process. You can ruin something accidentally. Botch, however, always implies clumsy or incompetent execution.
  • Bungle — almost a synonym for botch. Both mean to handle something clumsily and incompetently. "Bungle" is slightly more formal and is common in British English.
  • Fumble — more physical; it suggests awkward handling with the hands, like dropping a ball. Botch is broader and applies to any kind of task.
  • Mess up — very informal and general. "Mess up" can apply to almost anything going wrong. "Botch" is more specific — it always points to poor execution of a task.
  • Mishandle — more neutral and formal; it does not carry the same sense of incompetence or embarrassment that "botch" does.

"Botch" is an informal to semi-formal word. You will hear it in everyday conversation, and you will also see it in newspapers, news reports, and non-fiction writing. It is not slang, so it is perfectly acceptable in most written contexts. However, you would not typically use it in very formal academic writing — there, you might instead say "the procedure was carried out incorrectly" or "the task was mishandled."
To botch something is to carry out a task so badly — through carelessness, clumsiness, or incompetence — that the result is a failure or a mess, especially when it could have been done properly.
